To sneak means to move, do, or take something quietly and secretly, so that no one notices you. The key feeling behind "sneak" is hiding — you are deliberately trying to avoid being seen, heard, or caught.

It almost always carries a sense that what you're doing is not allowed, disapproved of, or at least something others wouldn't like if they knew.

1. To move somewhere secretly

This is about how you physically move — quietly, carefully, without drawing attention — because you don't want to be noticed.

  • A teenager sneaks out of the house at night after their parents have gone to sleep.
  • She sneaked past the security guard without being noticed.
  • He sneaked into the cinema without buying a ticket.
  • The cat sneaked under the bed the moment it heard the vet's voice.

Notice the feeling: the person knows they shouldn't be there, or knows someone would stop them if they were seen. That awareness of guilt or stealth is built into the word.

2. To do something, take something, or bring something secretly

Here, "sneak" is not always about physical movement from place to place. It's about doing an action — quickly, quietly, hoping nobody sees — because it's forbidden or frowned upon.

  • She sneaked a cookie from the jar when her mom wasn't looking.
  • He sneaked a glance at her phone while she wasn't looking. (looked quickly and secretly)
  • They sneaked a cigarette behind the school building.
  • She managed to sneak her phone into the exam hall.

Again, the core idea is the same: doing something you're not supposed to, or at least something you'd rather no one knew about.

This phrase means to approach someone (or something) so quietly and carefully that they don't notice you until you are very close.

  • He sneaked up on his friend and shouted "Boo!" — his friend nearly had a heart attack.
  • Don't sneak up on me like that! You scared me.

Interestingly, "sneak up on" is also used figuratively — meaning something happens gradually, without you realizing it, until it's already upon you:

  • Old age has a way of sneaking up on you.
  • The deadline sneaked up on me — I didn't realize it was so close.
  • Exhaustion sneaked up on her during the long drive.

Understanding the emotional colour of this word is just as important as knowing its definition.

  • Sneaking is almost never neutral. It implies guilt, shame, or at least a knowledge that you're doing something wrong — or something others wouldn't approve of.
  • If you use "sneak" to describe your own action, you are admitting that you knew it wasn't entirely proper. "I sneaked another slice of cake" — there's a playful, slightly guilty admission in this.
  • If you use it to describe someone else's action, it often carries a judgmental or accusatory tone: "He sneaked into the meeting" suggests he wasn't supposed to be there.
  • That said, it can be used in a light-hearted, harmless way too — sneaking a peek at a birthday present, sneaking an extra scoop of ice cream. The wrongdoing doesn't have to be serious.

Sneaking is typically a small-scale, personal act of stealth. It's not the word you'd use for a large military operation or a corporate scheme. Those would use words like "infiltrate" or "plot." "Sneak" feels human-sized — something a person does quietly, in a moment, often on impulse.

The secrecy in "sneak" is specifically about not wanting to be caught in the act. Compare:

  • "He walked quietly" — just describes his manner of walking. No hidden agenda.
  • "He sneaked" — he was deliberately trying not to be detected. There's intent behind the quietness.

The quietness is a tool he is using to avoid detection. That's what makes it "sneak" and not just "walk softly."

Here are the most natural ways "sneak" is used:

  • sneak in / sneak into — enter a place secretly (sneak into a party)
  • sneak out / sneak out of — leave a place secretly (sneak out of the office early)
  • sneak past — pass by someone without being noticed
  • sneak away / sneak off — leave quietly without anyone noticing (He sneaked away from the boring event)
  • sneak up on — approach silently until very close (physical or figurative)
  • sneak a look / sneak a peek / sneak a glance — look at something quickly and secretly
  • sneak a [food/drink] — eat or drink something secretly
  • sneak something in/out — bring something into or take it out of a place secretly

Both are correct, and you'll hear both. "Sneaked" is the standard, traditional past tense. "Snuck" is very common in informal American English and widely accepted.

  • She sneaked out last night. ✓
  • She snuck out last night. ✓ (informal, especially American)

To sneak is to move, act, or take something quietly and in secret, specifically to avoid being noticed, usually because what you're doing is not allowed or disapproved of. The word always carries a sense of deliberate concealment and usually a hint of guilt or mischief.
